# Book III, Proposition 18

*The straight line from the centre is perpendicular to the tangent*

> If a straight line touch a circle, and a straight line be joined from the centre to the point of contact, the straight line so joined will be perpendicular to the tangent.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/18-idea.svg" alt="The straight line from the centre to the point of contact (black) stands at right angles (yellow) to the straight line touching the circle (red). Every other straight line from the centre to it (dashed) ends outside the circle, and is longer." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>The straight line from the centre to the point of contact (black) stands at right angles (yellow) to the straight line touching the circle (red). Every other straight line from the centre to it (dashed) ends outside the circle, and is longer.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/18.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.18, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For let a straight line DE touch the circle ABC at the point C, let the centre F of the circle ABC be taken, and let FC be joined from F to C;

I say that FC is perpendicular to DE.

For, if not, let FG be drawn from F perpendicular to DE.

Then, since the angle FGC is right,

the angle FCG is acute; [I. 17]

and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side; [I. 19]

therefore FC is greater than FG.

But FC is equal to FB;

therefore FB is also greater than FG,

the less than the greater: which is impossible.

Therefore FG is not perpendicular to DE.

Similarly we can prove that neither is any other straight line except FC;

therefore FC is perpendicular to DE.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookIII/Prop18.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Prop18.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- If a straight line touch a circle, and a straight line be joined from the centre to the point of
contact, the straight line so joined will be perpendicular to the tangent. -/
theorem Prop18 {C D E F : Point} {ABC : Circle} (hF : Centre F ABC) (hC : OnCircle C ABC)
    (hDE : Touches D E ABC) (hCDE : Collinear D E C) :
    ∀ P : Point, Collinear D E P → P ≠ C → ∠ F C P = ∟ := by
  -- For let a straight line DE touch the circle ABC at the point C, let the centre F of the
  -- circle ABC be taken, and let FC be joined from F to C;
  /- The centre is within the circle, and no point of DE is, so F is off DE. -/
  have hF_DE : ¬ Collinear D E F := fun h => hDE.not_inside h (centre_inside hF)
  obtain ⟨L, hD_L, hE_L⟩ := Postulate1 D E hDE.1
  have hC_L : OnLine C L := by
    obtain ⟨M, hD_M, hE_M, hC_M⟩ := hCDE
    exact (line_unique hDE.1 hD_M hE_M hD_L hE_L) ▸ hC_M
  have hF_L : ¬ OnLine F L := fun h => hF_DE ⟨L, hD_L, hE_L, h⟩
  -- I say that FC is perpendicular to DE.
  -- For, if not, let FG be drawn from F perpendicular to DE.
  obtain ⟨G, hG, hFG⟩ := BookI.Prop12 hDE.1 hF_DE
  have hG_L : OnLine G L := by
    obtain ⟨M, hD_M, hE_M, hG_M⟩ := hG
    exact (line_unique hDE.1 hD_M hE_M hD_L hE_L) ▸ hG_M
  have hGC : G = C := Classical.byContradiction fun hGC => by
    -- Then, since the angle FGC is right,
    have hFGC : ∠ F G C = ∟ := hFG C hCDE (Ne.symm hGC)
    -- the angle FCG is acute; [I. 17]
    have hT : Triangle F G C := (Triangle.of_line hG_L hC_L hGC hF_L).bca.bca
    have hacute : ∠ G C F < ∟ := by
      have h17 := (BookI.Prop17 hT).1
      rw [hFGC] at h17
      exact Magnitude.lt_of_add_lt_add_left h17
    -- and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side; [I. 19]
    -- therefore FC is greater than FG.
    have hFG_FC : ‖F G‖ < ‖F C‖ := BookI.Prop19 hT (by rw [hFGC]; exact hacute)
    -- But FC is equal to FB;
    /- B is where FG leaves the circle. G is outside: no point of DE is within,
       and G cannot be on the circle, or DE would meet it at both C and G. -/
    have hG_out : OutsideCircle G ABC :=
      ⟨hDE.not_inside hG, fun hG_on =>
        (hDE.2 L hD_L hE_L).2 ⟨C, G, Ne.symm hGC, hC_L, hC, hG_L, hG_on⟩⟩
    obtain ⟨M, hF_M, hG_M⟩ := Postulate1 F G (fun e => hF_L (e ▸ hG_L))
    obtain ⟨B, hB, -, hFBG⟩ := line_circle_between (centre_inside hF) hF_M hG_out hG_M
    have hFC_FB : ‖F C‖ = ‖F B‖ := Definition15 hF hC hB
    -- therefore FB is also greater than FG,
    have hFG_FB : ‖F G‖ < ‖F B‖ := hFC_FB ▸ hFG_FC
    -- the less than the greater: which is impossible.
    exact lt_irrefl _ (lt_trans hFG_FB (len_lt_of_between hFBG))
  -- Therefore FG is not perpendicular to DE.
  -- Similarly we can prove that neither is any other straight line except FC;
  -- therefore FC is perpendicular to DE.
  subst hGC
  exact hFG
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

**"The less than the greater."** Euclid shows that FC is perpendicular to DE by showing that no other straight line from F is. If FG were perpendicular, the right angle at G would make FC greater than FG (I.17, I.19); but FC is equal to FB, and FB is only part of FG. We keep Heath's figure, which draws what cannot be: DE touches at C, and FG stands for the supposed perpendicular, with no right angle at G.

**"Two partial converses."** Heath reads III.18 and III.19 together: "Just as III. 3 contains two *partial* converses of the Porism to III. 1, so the present proposition and the next give two partial converses of the corollary to III. 16" (vol. 2, p. 45). His three things are a straight line touching the circle, a straight line from the centre to the point of contact, and right angles there: the porism gives the first from the other two, III.18 the third from the first two, and III.19 the second from the first and third. His note on the enunciation gives the Greek for "the tangent", ἡ ἐφαπτομένη (vol. 2, p. 45), a participle that names the straight line by what it does: touching.

**Where does B come from?** Euclid's figure puts B on FG between F and G, where FG leaves the circle. Lean asks why G is outside the circle at all. It cannot be within, since no point of a straight line that touches is within; and it cannot be on the circle, or DE would meet the circle at both C and G, and so cut it. With G outside, we find B with `line_circle_between`: a straight line from a point within a circle to a point outside crosses it between them. Euclid gives no citation for drawing FG: it is I.12, and once its foot proves to be C, FC is at right angles to DE on both sides of C.

**The modern way.** The foot of the perpendicular from F to the straight line C + tv (v ≠ 0) is the point of it nearest F, at t = −(C − F)·v/|v|². If the straight line touches, none of its points is within the circle, so none is nearer F than C; the foot is C itself, t = 0, and (C − F)·v = 0.
